headline: Tech earnings split the tape after hours: Amazon surged on an AWS cloud beat while Apple slid on weak guidance, as Thursday's cash session closed sharply higher on Microsoft's 16% surge and softer-than-expected June PCE data.
stance: The macro backdrop is genuinely two-sided heading into Friday. Thursday's June PCE print — headline down to 3.7% year-over-year, core at 3.3% — offered the market a brief reprieve, and equities used it: the S&P 500 closed up 1.7% at 7,437.63 (Thursday's cash close). But the Fed's 9-3 vote to hold, three dissents in favor of a hike, and Chair Warsh's explicit warning that rate increases "could well be part of the solution" keep the rate-hike risk alive. The post-close split between Amazon (~+8% after hours) and Apple (~-6% after hours) means index futures face conflicting forces at the open — neither story cleanly dominates, and the 30-year yield continues to hover near its post-2007 high.

news.head: Fed holds, three dissent
news.body: The Federal Reserve left its benchmark rate at 3.5%–3.75% on Wednesday, but three regional presidents voted for a 25-basis-point hike, and Chair Warsh said higher rates "could well be part of the solution" to bring inflation down — keeping September hike risk squarely on the table.

news.head: June PCE cools but stays hot
news.body: The Fed's preferred inflation gauge fell 0.1% in June, pulling the year-over-year rate to 3.7% from May's 4.1%; core PCE came in at 3.3% year-over-year — in line with forecasts, but nearly double the 2% target, and driven largely by a temporary Iran ceasefire that has since broken down.

news.head: Q2 GDP misses at 1.5%
news.body: Second-quarter GDP growth slowed to a 1.5% annualized rate, below expectations, with the shortfall traced mainly to a decline in federal government spending and inventories rather than any broad deterioration in private demand.

news.head: Amazon ~+8% after hours on AWS beat
news.body: Amazon reported Q2 net sales of $200.6 billion, up 20% year-over-year and ahead of estimates, with cloud revenue accelerating for the fifth straight quarter — shares jumped roughly 8% in extended trading after Thursday's close.

news.head: Apple ~-6% after hours on weak guidance
news.body: Apple's fiscal Q3 revenue came in at $109.4 billion — a slight beat — but the stock slid roughly 6% in extended trading after the company flagged a weaker-than-expected revenue outlook and deepening supply constraints.

news.head: Microsoft adds ~$450bn in a single session
news.body: Microsoft surged 16% in Thursday's cash session after reporting Azure-driven cloud growth that beat expectations, adding roughly $450 billion in market value — the single largest one-day gain by any stock on record — and pulling the information-technology sector up nearly 5% for the day.

news.head: US strikes Iran, ceasefire stalled
news.body: US forces carried out fresh strikes on Iranian targets after Tehran attacked American assets in the region; both sides remain deadlocked over the Strait of Hormuz, sustaining elevated energy-price and inflation risk.

implications: The 9-3 Fed dissent means the next meeting is live: markets are now pricing roughly a 63% probability of a September rate hike — a meaningful jump from the sub-56% level seen just before the decision.

June PCE cooling was real but mechanically energy-driven, and the energy disinflationary impulse reverses if Iran hostilities resume in July — the Q2 quarterly PCE price index surged 5.1% annualized, a reminder of the pipeline still building.

Thursday's tech-led rally (+1.7% SPX) was narrow: the information-technology sector carried nearly all the weight via Microsoft; the Apple after-hours drop (~-6%) and its roughly 7% index weight could restrain the Nasdaq at Friday's open.

Positioning: Speculators flipped to an extended long in S&P 500 futures this week — reaching the 85th percentile of their 3-year positioning range, a contrarian-bearish signal on a one-to-four-week horizon — while simultaneously cutting volatility protection to a 3-year low (VIX futures at the 10th percentile short, a contrarian-bullish lean on implied vol). The combination means the index is fully priced for calm; any shock reprices both legs at once.

Brent crude entered a new elevated-crowding extreme this week at $89.45/bbl (Thursday's cash close) — the first such reading in recent sessions — consistent with geopolitical risk being freshly priced in energy rather than fading.

watch.head: Employment Cost Index (8:30am ET)
watch.body: The Q2 Employment Cost Index lands before the open — a hot print would add fuel to the September hike debate and could push the long end of the yield curve higher.

watch.head: Chicago PMI & Michigan Sentiment (9:45 / 10am ET)
watch.body: End-of-month sentiment and regional activity data round out the week; a soft Michigan inflation-expectations reading would be the most market-moving outcome given the current rate debate.

watch.head: Apple and Amazon opening prints
watch.body: With Apple down ~6% and Amazon up ~8% after hours, watch whether index-level moves offset at the open or whether Apple's larger weight tips the Nasdaq lower — and whether Amazon's AWS enthusiasm spills into broader cloud and AI names.

watch.head: 30-year yield and the 2007 high
watch.body: The long bond has been trading near its highest level since 2007 post-Fed; any further push higher would tighten financial conditions and pressure duration-sensitive equities and real estate.

watch.head: Bank of Japan decision
watch.body: The BOJ is widely expected to hold rates unchanged; any surprise shift in language on yield-curve control could jolt the yen — which closed Thursday at 159.55 per dollar (Thursday's cash close), its weakest range in nearly three years.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: The single biggest change since Thursday's open: June PCE printed -0.1% month-over-month, pulling the year-over-year rate to 3.7% from 4.1% in May — yet Chair Warsh said the cooler data "did not factor significantly" into the hold decision, and three FOMC members dissented for a hike; markets now price roughly a 63% chance of a September increase.
Q2 GDP advanced at a 1.5% annualized rate — below expectations — with the miss concentrated in government spending and inventories; private consumption held up, with real PCE +0.4% in June.

The 10-year Treasury closed Thursday at 4.68% (Thursday's cash close); the 2-year at 4.23% (Thursday's cash close), leaving the 2s10s curve at +45 basis points — still positive but narrowed by the hike-risk repricing.
The 30-year yield is hovering near its highest level since 2007 following the Fed decision — an ongoing constraint on mortgage rates, capex financing, and long-duration equity valuations.

Real rates (10-year TIPS-implied) closed at 2.41% Thursday — a level that historically compresses equity multiples; the Shiller CAPE at 40.6x means the margin of safety against further rate increases is thin.
Gold closed Thursday at $4,162.80/oz; overnight (~6am ET) it was printing near $4,086 — reflecting a reassessment of Fed hike odds offsetting the geopolitical bid.
US-Iran hostilities continued overnight, with fresh American strikes reported; Tehran's insistence on Strait of Hormuz control keeps a sustained energy-price floor under inflation.
sections.positioning: Speculators hold almost no bullish bets left in 3M SOFR interest-rate futures — a 3-year low and a contrarian-bullish lean for front-end rates — but this positioning has been in place for 14 straight weeks and is background context rather than a fresh signal.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: The S&P 500 closed Thursday at 7,437.63 (+1.7%), the Nasdaq Composite at 25,122.18 (+2.8%), and the Dow at 52,208.06 (+1.2%) — all prior cash closes.

Microsoft's 16% single-session gain drove information technology to its best day since April 2025, accounting for the bulk of the index move; breadth was narrow, with about 65% of S&P 500 members above their 50-day moving average as of Wednesday.

Apple (~-6% after hours) reported fiscal Q3 revenue of $109.4 billion — a slight beat — but a weaker forward revenue outlook and supply-chain constraints drove the after-hours drop; Apple's roughly 7% S&P 500 weight means Friday's open will feel it.

Amazon (~+8% after hours) posted Q2 net sales of $200.6 billion, up 20% year-over-year, with AWS cloud revenue accelerating for the fifth straight quarter — the cleanest AI-infrastructure proof point from the megacap cohort this cycle.

VIX closed Thursday at 17.09 (Thursday's cash close) — an elevated-complacency reading given the rate backdrop; skew at 139.9 shows the options market is pricing tail risk more actively than the VIX headline suggests.
Breadth split: about 49% of Nasdaq 100 members are above their 50-day moving average (as of Wednesday's close), meaning the index rally is being driven by a relatively small number of large names.
sections.positioning: NEW this week: speculators flipped to an extended long in S&P 500 futures — 85th percentile of the 3-year range, a contrarian-bearish warning — while simultaneously cutting their volatility (VIX futures) protection to a 3-year low (10th percentile short, a contrarian-bullish lean on implied vol). Both moves are new in the current week. Separately, speculators have almost no bullish bets left in Russell 2000 futures — near a 3-year low — a contrarian-bullish lean for small-caps, though that position has been in place for 13 weeks and is background context.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: High-yield spreads closed at 287 basis points over investment grade (as of Tuesday's close) — elevated but not signaling stress; investment-grade option-adjusted spreads were 81 basis points (Tuesday's close).

Short-term funding stress gauges remain quiet: FRA-OIS and SOFR-OIS both sat at 2 basis points (Tuesday's close), and the commercial paper funding spread was 18 basis points (as of July 24) — no signs of wholesale funding pressure.

Bank reserves at $2,984.6 billion and the Treasury General Account at $910.8 billion (both as of Wednesday) leave system liquidity ample; the overnight reverse-repo facility has essentially drained to $1.1 billion (Thursday's close), removing a former buffer.

The 10-year breakeven inflation rate closed Thursday at 2.27%, well below the realized PCE readings — suggesting the bond market expects energy-driven inflation to partially reverse, though the ongoing Iran conflict is a material upside risk to that assumption.

The equity-credit correlation at 0.70 (Thursday's close) means risk-off episodes in bonds and stocks are moving together — a diversification headwind for balanced portfolios if the rate-hike narrative reasserts.
